payload.stem: Two carts of equal mass $0.5\text{ kg}$ at rest on a frictionless track are pushed apart by a compressed spring between them. The spring releases a total of $6\text{ J}$ of energy, which becomes kinetic energy of the carts, and the carts have equal kinetic energy because their masses are equal: $3.00\text{ J}$ each. In a second trial one of the carts is replaced by a cart with $2$ times the mass, and the spring releases the same $6\text{ J}$. What is the best prediction of the kinetic energy of the lighter cart in the second trial?

options.why: Gives all of the energy to the lighter cart.
Momentum is conserved, so $mv_1=(2m)v_2$ and $v_1=2v_2$. The kinetic energies are in the ratio $K_1:K_2=2:1$, so the lighter cart has the fraction $2/(2+1)$ of $6\text{ J}$, which is $4.00\text{ J}$.
Gives the lighter cart the inverse share, $E/(1+f)$.
Gives the lighter cart the same share as before, ignoring the larger mass of the other cart.

payload.stem: In a hydraulic lift a small piston of area $2\text{ cm}^2$ is pushed down with a force of $20\text{ N}$ through a distance of $0.3\text{ m}$. The incompressible fluid transmits the pressure to a large piston of area $20\text{ cm}^2$. Friction is negligible. Which statement about the work done on the small piston and by the fluid on the large piston is correct and best justified?

options.text: The work done on the large piston is less than the work done on the small piston, because the fluid loses energy transmitting the force.
options.why: Assumes that energy is lost in the fluid even though friction is negligible and the fluid is incompressible.

options.text: The work done on the large piston is $10$ times as great, because the force on it is $10$ times as great.
options.why: Multiplies the work by the force factor without noticing that the large piston moves a proportionally smaller distance.

options.text: The work done on the small piston is $10$ times as great, because the small piston must be pushed with more pressure.
options.why: Confuses the pressure in the fluid with the force; the pressure is the same on both pistons.

options.text: The work is the same for both pistons, $6.00\text{ J}$, because the large piston gets a force $10$ times as great but moves only $1/10$ of the distance, so the force and distance changes cancel.
options.why: The pressure is equal, so $F_2=200\text{ N}$; the fluid volume is conserved, so $d_2=d_1/10=0.0300\text{ m}$; then $W_2=F_2d_2=6.00\text{ J}=W_1$.

payload.explanation_en:
The correct answer is The work is the same for both pistons, $9.00\text{ J}$, because the large piston gets a force $20$ times as great but moves only $1/20$ of the distance, so the force and distance changes cancel.. The pressure is equal, so $F_2=600\text{ N}$; the fluid volume is conserved, so $d_2=d_1/20=0.0150\text{ m}$; then $W_2=F_2d_2=9.00\text{ J}=W_1$.
The work done on the large piston is $20$ times as great, because the force on it is $20$ times as great. is incorrect: Multiplies the work by the force factor without noticing that the large piston moves a proportionally smaller distance.
The work done on the large piston is less than the work done on the small piston, because the fluid loses energy transmitting the force. is incorrect: Assumes that energy is lost in the fluid even though friction is negligible and the fluid is incompressible.
The work done on the small piston is $20$ times as great, because the small piston must be pushed with more pressure. is incorrect: Confuses the pressure in the fluid with the force; the pressure is the same on both pistons.

payload.stem: In a hydraulic lift a small piston of area $2\text{ cm}^2$ is pushed down with a force of $20\text{ N}$ through a distance of $0.2\text{ m}$. The incompressible fluid transmits the pressure to a large piston of area $40\text{ cm}^2$. Friction is negligible. Which statement about the work done on the small piston and by the fluid on the large piston is correct and best justified?

options.text: The work done on the small piston is $20$ times as great, because the small piston must be pushed with more pressure.
options.why: Confuses the pressure in the fluid with the force; the pressure is the same on both pistons.

options.text: The work done on the large piston is less than the work done on the small piston, because the fluid loses energy transmitting the force.
options.why: Assumes that energy is lost in the fluid even though friction is negligible and the fluid is incompressible.

options.text: The work is the same for both pistons, $4.00\text{ J}$, because the large piston gets a force $20$ times as great but moves only $1/20$ of the distance, so the force and distance changes cancel.

options.text: The work done on the large piston is $20$ times as great, because the force on it is $20$ times as great.
options.why: Multiplies the work by the force factor without noticing that the large piston moves a proportionally smaller distance.
